requirements.requirement: Every command run through sudo on node1 is recorded with user and timestamp to /var/log/sudo-commands.log
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook installed a sudoers drop-in (Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo-commands.log"; Defaults log_year) and created the log file (root:root 0600). Direct verification shows entries with timestamp, user, PWD, USER, and COMMAND fields for a variety of subsequent sudo invocations (id -u, systemctl, tail, ls, wc, grep). The setting is a global sudoers Default, applying to all sudo invocations, not scoped to one user.

requirements.requirement: Sudo log entries are kept out of the general system log (auth.log)
requirements.summary: Defaults !syslog was added via the sudoers drop-in. Before the change, auth.log had 6 pre-existing COMMAND= entries from baseline testing; after applying the change, multiple additional sudo commands were run and auth.log's COMMAND= count remained frozen at 6 across two separate verification passes, while only unrelated PAM session open/close lines continued to appear there.

Ansible was installed (ansible-core 2.16.3 / ansible 9.2.0) and a playbook.yml was authored with file and sudoers-copy (validate=visudo) tasks; ansible-playbook was executed against localhost with connection=local, completing changed=2/failed=0.

requirements.requirement: Sudo logging configuration persists and functions correctly across a node1 restart
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline (boot_id f9bf293d, working sudoers config) was captured, a restart was acknowledged and confirmed via a subsequent connection timeout, the node was polled back to reachable with a changed boot_id (2a6d52aa), and a post-reboot functional check confirmed the sudoers drop-in, log file, and logging behavior (auth.log COMMAND= count still frozen at 6) survived the reboot.

overall_summary: The task's three material outcomes are all directly and concretely satisfied: an Ansible playbook (run locally on node1) installed a sudoers drop-in that redirects and formats sudo command logging to /var/log/sudo-commands.log with user/timestamp fields, and disabled syslog forwarding for sudo, verified by a frozen auth.log COMMAND= count against a growing dedicated log across multiple checks, including after a full node1 restart that changed the boot identity and confirmed configuration and behavior survived intact. The independently-required provider-wide restart protocol was also completed on both node1 and node2 with clear pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement (confirmed via connection timeout), new boot identity, and recovered health/functionality, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. The main hygiene note is installing ansible directly on node1 (rather than driving the change from the pre-provisioned node2 ansible-controller) and a few small unreverted temp files, neither of which affects functional correctness or introduces risk.
limitations: No direct evidence was captured showing whether node2 could reach node1 over SSH/inventory before the executor chose a local-connection approach on node1 instead, so it cannot be confirmed whether installing ansible on node1 was avoidable.

Lifecycle snapshots do not include a direct /var/log/sudo-commands.log or sudoers content capture (they are fixed generic observations), so cross-checking task-specific final state relies solely on the executor's own captured command outputs.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing executor commands. apt-get update/install of ansible on node1 (cmd-5c904bb3b58846f7, cmd-ff36a126b27f4a9b) was a necessary prerequisite for the chosen local-connection implementation approach, though it deviates from the provisioned topology where node2 carries the dedicated ansible-controller image and node1 does not — this leaves an unrequested ansible installation and its dependency footprint on the target node rather than driving the change remotely from node2; this is low-risk, non-destructive residue rather than an unnecessary experiment, so it is only lightly penalized. The playbook file and its early rsyslog-stat draft (cmd-727793a8cc6b4ff6) were superseded before execution and never applied (only the revised version in cmd-d3c1a4b0a16b437c was run), so no wasted mutation occurred there. Minor leftover artifacts remain unreverted: /tmp/ansible-sudo-log/playbook.yml and /tmp/apt-update.log, /tmp/apt-install.log, /tmp/reboot.log — all low-risk temp files with no security or functional impact. Both node1 and node2 restarts were bounded, low-risk, and necessary for the independent restart-evidence protocol; no failed services, damaged package state, or new unsafe network exposure were observed in the lifecycle snapshots (added/removed listening-socket and /tmp lines are attributable to normal reboot churn, e.g. new ephemeral systemd-private dirs and a DHCP UDP socket, not executor-introduced exposure).
